tagline.text: A pig's-spine ridge overlooking the sea at Anilao

location.label: Location
location.text: Anilao, Calumpang Peninsula, Mabini, Batangas (around Brgy. Ligaya)

duration.label: Time needed
duration.text: Half day to a full day

budget.label: Budget
budget.text: About ₱800–1,800 (day hike from Manila, sharing guide fees)

children.text: Mount Gulugod Baboy is a ridge mountain of about 525 m on the Mabini peninsula where Anilao sits. As its name, "pig's spine," suggests, a long grassy ridge looks down on the Verde Island Passage and Sombrero Island, making it an ideal half-day hike during a dive trip.
Gulugod Baboy sits on the Calumpang Peninsula in the Anilao area of Mabini, Batangas. In Tagalog, gulugod means spine and baboy means pig; the ridge is said to resemble a pig's backbone. It is about
105 km
south of Manila, so a half-day hike fits easily into a trip to the dive resorts of Anilao.

The mountain is described as having three peaks: Gulugod Baboy Peak (about 470 m), Gitna Peak in the middle (about 485 m), and the highest, Pinagbanderahan (about 525 m). Hikers often call the 525 m peak the true Gulugod Baboy, while locals call it Pinagbanderahan. The name means "the place where the flag was raised." One guide tells of surviving airmen planting a flag there when a Japanese aircraft crashed on the slope during World War II, and of flags being raised again when Batangas was liberated in April 1945.
The hike is easy. Hiking sites classify it as a difficulty 2/9 minor climb with trail class 1–2. A recent guide describes about
out and back, with
2–3 hours
up and
1.5–2 hours

down (older accounts say 1–2 hours to the summit, so times vary a lot with the person and the route). The start is a steep concrete road, followed by clay paths through secondary forest and then shadeless grassland.

The scenery is the main attraction. From the ridge you can see the Verde Island Passage, Sombrero and Maricaban islands, Batangas Bay, and, far off, Mindoro and Mount Maculot. Because the mountain rises right behind Anilao, many people climb in the morning and return to diving or the beach in the afternoon. It is also grazing land for cattle and goats, and parts of the trail cross private property, so follow the rules and be courteous.
The highlight is the ridge path linking Gulugod Baboy Peak, Gitna Peak and Pinagbanderahan Peak. One guide's sample plan crosses all three and descends in about
3 hours
. The path between the peaks keeps rising and falling, so pace your energy.

blocks.title: View of the Verde Island Passage

children.text: From the ridge you look down on the Verde Island Passage, Sombrero Island and Maricaban Island. On clear days Mindoro is faintly visible far away, and on the other side you can see Batangas City, Mount Maculot, Mount Batulao and the Tagaytay highlands.

From the middle of the hike onward the trail is shadeless cogon grassland. The wind is steady and cool, but the sun is direct, so a hat and sunscreen are essential. In the dry season the grass burns easily, and open fires are reportedly prohibited.
Ask your guide about the wartime story behind the peak's name. Accounts of the plane crash and the flag raised at liberation differ from guide to guide, so enjoy it as a story.
There is a campsite below the summit where you can stay overnight. A 2026 guide lists camping at about
per person. The wind is strong, so stake your tent down firmly.
A paved road is said to reach an upper parking lot just below the summit. The walk from the lot to the summit is about
10–15 minutes
, so even travelers who cannot hike far can reach the top. The road is steep with hairpin turns, so drive carefully.
Anilao is one of the Philippines' leading dive areas. You can plan two days: spend the morning on the hike and rest in the afternoon, or dive the next day. Divers pay a separate local sanctuary fee.
Sombrero Island, visible from the summit, can be reached from Anilao by boat. Combining a visit to the island with the day after your hike is a popular plan.

The dry season from November to May is the best time to climb, and December to February is said to have the most pleasant temperatures. If you start early in the morning, there are fewer people and the sun is weaker.
In the rainy season from June to October, the clay trail is slippery and the descent is especially risky; cloud can also hide the view. Typhoons or heavy rain can suddenly halt hiking.
It gets crowded during Holy Week, Christmas and long weekends, so weekdays or a dawn start are recommended.

There is no fixed closure period, but hiking can be halted without notice during typhoons or heavy rain. Check the forecast and Mabini disaster-response notices before you leave, and allow extra descent time in the rainy season.

Anilao, at the foot of the mountain, is full of dive resorts, so there are many places to stay. Rooms and meals vary greatly by resort and prices are wide-ranging, so check booking sites for your dates. A day hike is possible by leaving Manila before dawn and returning in the afternoon, but staying a night in Anilao makes the schedule far more relaxed.

Places to eat near the summit are limited. A small shop at the start is said to be the last place to buy water before the ridge, so bring water and snacks in advance. After the hike, you can eat seafood and Filipino home cooking at restaurants near Anilao Port or at the resorts. Most places are reported to take cash only, so carry plenty of small bills. Mobile signal is good at the trailhead but can be unreliable or absent near the campsite, so tell family or your lodging your plan and the time you expect to be down.
Registration, guides, environmental fees and tolls are often paid in cash. Bring small bills.
Carry
2–3 liters
of water. Guides say there are no refill points on the mountain.
The clay is slippery for a day or more after rain, so shoes with good grip and trekking poles are best.
Bring a hat, sunscreen, a long-sleeved UPF shirt and an umbrella. Most of the ridge has no shade.
Insects increase at dusk, so carry repellent if you camp around sunset.
Even in a large group, follow your guide; the trail forks often and markings are said to be inconsistent.
If you plan around the storm season, check with the Mabini municipal office or disaster-response office about whether hiking is possible.
Carry out all your trash. Single-use plastic bags are reportedly banned by local ordinance.
Registration is walk-in only, with no online booking or daily quota, and the desk reportedly opens around

There is a risk of lightning and heat stroke on the shadeless ridge, and the clay trail is very slippery in the rainy season. Change your plans if the weather is bad.
Lightning is dangerous on the ridge. If the sky darkens, come down.
The trail crosses private land with many grazing cattle. Avoid the cows and their droppings and do not damage fences.
Stray dogs have been reported in some areas. Do not feed them and keep your distance.
The cogon grass catches fire easily in the dry season, so do not light fires or smoke.
Fees and rules change every year. Check the latest information with Mabini tourism or a local guide before you go.
